lead: A permutation counts ordered arrangements; a combination counts unordered selections. The same set of objects gives different answers when order matters and when it does not. This distinction is the core of counting: it tells you whether to multiply by r! or not, whether repeats are allowed, and whether the arrangement sits on a line or a circle. It appears in PIN and password rules, lottery and team selection, seating plans, and in the binomial coefficients used throughout computer science.
prereq: You need: the product rule from 3.1 Counting rules, and Unit 2 on functions if you want the permutation-function view.

blocks.text: A permutation is an ordered arrangement of r objects chosen from n distinct objects. The two-letter words AB and BA use the same letters but are different permutations. Use permutations when positions, ranks or roles differ.

blocks.where: nPr is the number of ordered arrangements of r objects from n distinct objects; n! = n × (n − 1) × ... × 1; 0! = 1; 0 ≤ r ≤ n.

blocks.text: The formula is the product rule: n choices for the first position, n − 1 for the second, down to n − r + 1 for the last. If repetition is allowed, each of the r positions has n choices, so the count is n<sup>r</sup>. If repetition is forbidden, you cannot use n<sup>r</sup>.

A circular permutation fixes rotations. Seat n distinct people around a round table: fix one person to break the rotation, then arrange the remaining n − 1 people in a line. The count is (n − 1)!. If clockwise and anticlockwise orders are also considered the same, as with a necklace, divide by 2 for n ≥ 3; check the wording before doing this.
A permutation of all n objects is a bijection from a set to itself; see Unit 2 on functions. The factorial n! is its count.

A combination is an unordered selection of r objects from n distinct objects. Choosing questions 1, 2 and 3 is the same as choosing 3, 2 and 1. Some syllabi call selections combinations and arrangements permutations.

blocks.where: nCr is the number of r-object subsets of an n-object set; the order of the r objects is ignored.

blocks.text: Link to permutations: nPr = r! × nCr, because each chosen set of r objects can be ordered in r! ways. Example: C(10,3) = 120; P(10,3) = 720 = 6 × 120. The identities C(n,r)=C(n,n−r) and C(n,r)=C(n−1,r−1)+C(n−1,r) follow by counting subsets.

Combinatorial proof of C(n,r)=C(n,n−r): choosing r objects to keep is the same as choosing n−r objects to leave out. Both actions describe the same subset, so the counts are equal. For Pascal's identity, split the subsets by one fixed object: either it is included, giving C(n−1,r−1), or excluded, giving C(n−1,r).

Combinations with repetition: choose r items from n types when repeats are allowed and order is ignored. Put r identical stars and n−1 dividers in a row; the count is C(n+r−1,r). Example: 3 scoops from 5 flavours, repeats allowed, gives C(7,3)=35.

A multiset has repeated objects. The number of distinct arrangements of n objects with k types, where type i appears n_i times, is n! / (n_1! n_2! ... n_k!). Divide by each repeated factorial because swapping identical copies does not create a new arrangement.

blocks.where: n = n_1 + ... + n_k; n_i is the count of identical objects of type i.

blocks.text: Example: the letters of BANANA are 6 objects: B once, A three times, N twice. Arrangements = 6! / (1! 3! 2!) = 720 / 12 = 60. If all letters were distinct, the count would be 6! = 720; the division removes the invisible swaps.

Use a decision checklist: Does order matter? Are repeats allowed? Is the arrangement circular? For selections with repeats, use stars and bars; for arrangements with repeats, use the multiset formula. Write the count as a product of stages before simplifying factorials.

figure.caption: Four PIN slots show the choices: 9 for the first digit (0 is excluded), then 9, 8 and 7 for the remaining distinct digits; the product is 4536. Notice that the second slot still has 9 choices, because 0 becomes available.

spec.title: 4-digit PIN, distinct digits, first digit not 0
spec.aria: Four PIN slots show 9 choices for the first digit, then 9, 8 and 7 choices for the remaining distinct digits.

examples.question: A 4-digit PIN uses four different digits from 0–9 and cannot start with 0. How many PINs exist? Also, how many ways can a student choose 3 of 10 practice questions?
steps: First digit: digits 1 to 9, so 9 choices. 0 is not allowed here.
Second digit: any digit 0–9 except the first. That is 10 − 1 = 9 choices. Zero is now allowed.
Third digit: exclude the first two, so 10 − 2 = 8 choices. Fourth digit: 10 − 3 = 7 choices.
Practice questions: order does not matter, so use combinations. C(10,3) = 10! / (3! 7!) = (10 × 9 × 8) / (3 × 2 × 1) = 720 / 6 = 120.
examples.answer: There are 4536 four-digit PINs and 120 ways to choose 3 of 10 practice questions.
examples.check:
import math
pin = 9 * 9 * 8 * 7
questions = math.comb(10, 3)
print(pin)
print(questions)

traps: Using n<sup>r</sup> when repeats are forbidden. For a 4-digit PIN with distinct digits, the count is not 10<sup>4</sup>.
Forgetting that 0 cannot lead but can appear later. The first digit has 9 choices, not 10; the second digit has 9 choices, not 8.
Using permutations when selection order does not matter. Choosing 3 practice questions or a cricket team is a combination.
In circular seating, writing n! instead of (n − 1)!. Fix one person first to remove the repeated rotations.

quiz.q: Write the formula for the number of ordered arrangements of r objects from n distinct objects without repetition.

quiz.a: P(10,3) first counts ordered choices. Each 3-element subset appears in 3! orders, so divide by 3! to keep one representative per subset.

quiz.q: How many 3-letter codes can be made from A, B, C, D and E without repetition when order matters?
From 12 cricket players, how many ways can a team of 4 be chosen?
Six people sit around a round table. How many distinct arrangements are there, and why is 6! wrong?
quiz.a: (6 − 1)! = 120 arrangements. 6! counts each rotation as six different line-ups, but rotations are the same circular arrangement.

quiz.q: Give a combinatorial proof that C(n,r)=C(n,n−r).
quiz.a: Choosing r objects to keep is the same as choosing the n−r objects to leave out. Both choices describe the same subset, so the counts are equal.

quiz.q: How many distinct arrangements of the letters in BANANA are there?
quiz.a: There are 6 letters: A appears 3 times, N appears 2 times, B appears 1 time. Count = 6! / (3! 2! 1!) = 720 / (6 × 2) = 60.

beyond: Not for the exam. These counts power hashing and load balancing: choosing which bucket an item can occupy, or how many distinct keys fit in a bucket, uses combinations. Probability uses binomial coefficients C(n,r) for r successes in n trials. Algorithm analysis uses binomial and multinomial coefficients to count states and paths. Search next for stars and bars, multinomial coefficient, circular permutations, and binomial identities.
